item.title: Trump’s use of Russian diesel fuel, at Ukraine’s expense, sparks controversy in the US
item.description: Donald Trump’s plan to import Russian diesel despite Western sanctions has sparked fierce criticism in Washington, including from Republicans, as high fuel prices and the upcoming midterm elections put pressure on his administration. His approach to the Ukraine war has also drawn controversy, with calls for Kyiv to hold elections and claims of an energy ceasefire announced without clear agreement from the parties involved. item.title: US economists win Nobel for research helping policymakers navigate crises
item.description: Two American economists, Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, have won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on economic stabilisation. Their research helps policymakers and central banks better understand economic fluctuations, manage recessions and inflation, and account for public expectations when shaping economic policy. The prize money, worth around $1.2 million, will be shared equally between the two laureates.

item.title: Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’
item.description:
Cocaine seizures in Europe are up more than fivefold in 10 years as a host of cartels take root. A four-month Guardian investigation reveals the true scale of a continent-wide shift

A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations.

The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. Between 2014 and 2024, there was a 471% rise in the quantity of cocaine seized and more local laboratories processing cocaine derivatives were dismantled.

item.title: Brazil blames human action for the fires sweeping the Amazon
item.description: The Brazilian government has blamed deliberate human action for the wave of fires in Amazonas state, where 540 new hotspots were recorded in 48 hours, more than half of those detected in the whole of October 2025, according to the National Institute for Space Research. The situation has led to a state of emergency in 36 municipalities.

item.title: IMF trims Latin America’s outlook to 2.3% and sharply cuts Argentina’s
item.description: The International Monetary Fund has lowered its 2026 growth forecast for Latin America and the Caribbean to 2.3%, a tenth of a point less than in July, and sharply cut Argentina’s, from 3.5% to 2.1%. Chile and Uruguay are also among the region’s largest downward revisions, according to the World Economic Outlook presented on Monday in Bangkok, during the annual meetings of the Fund and the World Bank.

item.title: Argentina temporarily closes Iguazu Falls after El Niño-fuelled surge in water levels
item.description:
National park officials took the precautionary measure to limit tourist access after heavy rain caused the Iguazu River to flow at six times the normal rate

Heavy rainfall fuelled by a supersized El Niño weather pattern briefly forced Argentinian authorities to close tourist access to the famed Iguazu Falls, amid fears that rapidly rising water levels would cause the river to burst its banks.

National park officials took the precautionary measure on Monday when the Iguazu River’s flow exceeded 12,000 cubic metres per second – more than six times its average rate.

item.title: Two Years On, the Sinaloa Cartel War Changes Shape | The InSight Take
item.description:
Two Years On, the Sinaloa Cartel War Changes Shape | The InSight Take

Two years after Ismael Zambada Garcia, alias "El Mayo," was handed over to US authorities in what was deemed a traitorous act by one faction against another, the war between the Chapitos and the Mayiza factions of the Sinaloa Cartel continues to roil the area. The conflict has implications for the criminal superstructure throughout the country.

InSight Crime's Victoria Dittmar and co-director Steven Dudley were recently in Culiacán, Sinaloa, where they interviewed drug producers, residents, and local sources. They found a city where the war is less visible than it was but no less present.
